LOCAL MEAN TIME OF MOONRISE, 1944, LATITUDE 40° NORTH 

NOTE: This is not standard time. To reduce to standard time, decrease the local mean time by 4 for every degree the station is cast of the standard meridian, or increase the local mean time by 4m for every degree the station is west of the standard meridian. The times are inaccurate for other latitudes than the given one. The table is based on longitude 75° west, but can be used for other longitudes in the U. S. without much inaccuracy, a gradual increase in the tabulated times being given as one goes west from 75°, with a maximum of 6″ for stations on the Pacific coast. FOREWORD 

The special explanations and suggestions for the use of the AMERICAN 

ASTROLOGY EPHEMERIS AND ASPECTARIAN, which are the same from year to year, are incorporated in the companion compilation, the AMERICAN 

ASTROLOGY TABLES OF HOUSES, in order to conserve space in the annual publication, and make the yearly tables available at the lowest possible price. 

Most students of astrology are familiar with the details of an ephemeris, and will especially appreciate the use here of the natural division of the day, at midnight, and the computations for the 75° west meridian, since this requires the least amount of change for the charts used by American astrologers. Additional and detailed suggestions for the employment of these tabulations will be found in the book, THE DAILY USE OF THE EPHEMERIS, listed among the valuable helps for the student on the back cover. 

The symbols employed for the aspects in the ASPECTARIAN for 1944, and whose general interpretation is given in the AMERICAN ASTROLOGY TABLES OF HOUSES, are as follows. 

Conjunction, 0° y Semisextile, 30° 

4 Semisquare, 45° 

* Sextile, 60° 

☐ Square, 90° ▲ Trine, 120° || Parallel Sesquiquadrate, 135° 

Quincunx, 150° 

Opposition, 180°

SUNRISE Local Mean Time 

To change to standard time, increase the local meantime by 4m for every degree the station is west of the standard meridian, or decrease the local meantime by 4m for every degree the station is east of the standard meridian.

The American Astrology Aspectarian for 1944 Eastern Standard Time 

For Central Standard Time, subtract 1 from the given time; for Mountain Standard Time, subtract 2b; for Pacific 

Standard Time, subtract 3h. For "war time" (= daylight-saving time), add 1h to the standard time used by the individual. 

Example: find mountain war time for Denver, Col., Feb. 1, 1:30 a.m. EST; 1h30m 2h 11:30 p.m., Jan. 31, MST; add 

1h giving 0h30m MWT of Feb. 1.

The hours given may be accepted as a reliable guide if you will time your actions and decisions as closely as possible to the hour given. If it is not possible to act precisely at the hour indicated, a time should be chosen which is earlier rather than later.

ECLIPSES FOR 1944 

1. A total eclipse of the sun, January 25. The total phase is invisible in North America. The path of totality begins (at 8:45 am, E.S.T.) in the Pacific Ocean west of South America, a little north of the equator and considerably west of the Galápagos Islands. It enters the coast of South America at the northern part of Peru, at 

Aguja Point, cuts across northern Peru and across the northern border of Bolivia, crosses Brazil, and leaves the eastern coast at Fortaleza. The central line of totality then crosses the Atlantic Ocean, entering west Africa at the northern boundary of Sierra Leone, and ending in the middle of the Sahara region at 12:08 pm, E.S.T. The greatest duration of totality at any one place is 49, which occurs in the interior of Brazil, 500 miles south of the mouth of the Amazon River. The time of mid-eclipse here is 10:25 am, E.S.T. All of northern and central South 

America as well as Central America, are under the partial phases of the eclipse; while Mexico and the extreme southern part of the U.S. are under the partial eclipse for a short time after sunrise. At New Orleans, La., 180 of the sun is obscured, and at Panama City, of the sun is covered. In the eastern hemisphere, the partial phases (near sunset time) extend from the southern tip of England to Sicily and to central Africa. Conjunction in R. A. occurs at 10:29:17 am., E.S.T., and the sun's geocentric longitude at the time of new moon is 4°32'55". 

2. An annular eclipse of the sun, July 19-20. Invisible in the western hemisphere. The path of the annular phase begins (July 19, 10:47 pm, E.S.T.) in the Uganda district, north of Lake Victoria in east Africa, crosses

Ethiopia, and leaves the African coast south of the Gulf of Aden. The central line of the eclipse crosses the Arabian Sea and enters India at a point about 100 miles south of Bombay; it goes across the peninsula of India and the Bay of Bengal, and passes over Burma just north of Rangoon. It traverses Siam and leaves Asia at the coast of French Indo-China. It crosses the South China Sea and the Sulu Sea, and goes over the island of Mindanao of the Philippine Islands, passing over Catabato. It then goes into the Pacific Ocean, almost touching the northeast coast of New Guinea, crosses the southern part of New Britain Island and ends (July 20, 2:38 am, E.S.T.) at 

Bougainville of the Solomon Islands group. The greatest duration of the annular phase at any one place is 342", which occurs at a point at the Irrawaddi River, 200 miles nearly north of Rangoon. The time of mid-eclipse here is July 20, 0:40 am, E.S.T. The eastern part of Africa, the southern half of Asia, the north Indian Ocean, all but the southwestern part of Australia, all of the islands of Australasia, and the southern part of Japan as far as Tokyo, are under the partial phases. At Manila, P. I., 1 of the sun is obscured. Conjunction in right ascension occurs 

July 20, 0:43:09 am, E.S.T., and the sun's geocentric longitude at the time of new moon is 27°21′51".
